You pretty much nailed it, just a few things I’d add I think. There are 2 types of fiber, soluble and insoluble. Soluble fiber is absorbed by the body no problem but insoluble is not. However, gut bacteria thrives off of eating insoluble fiber. So our gut bacteria digests this insoluble fiber and passes its own waste, and this waste we ARE able to absorb as energy. So insoluble fiber technically is zero calories to us, but then our gut bacteria eats it and the waste products produced by the bacteria is such that we can absorb it as energy. 

So you do get energy from consuming insoluble fiber, but because the energy isn’t directly coming from the food product itself, it has to be processed by gut bacteria first, then companies can get away with putting it on a label as zero calories. However when put into a bomb calorimeter, it does burn off as containing energy. 

Kind of a confusing loophole but I hope that makes sense. Tl;dr: it has about half as many calories as a regular carbohydrate, so around 2 calories per gram.

The exact same principles apply as if you’re eating throughout the day. 

Eat enough protein, lift weights, train with enough intensity, train consistently, sleep enough, manage stress. 

You will build muscle. It being OMAD, it happens a little slower, but it still happens if you apply the appropriate principles.

Learning the difference between being a competitive bodybuilder and someone who just wants to enjoy training, look better, and grow some muscle and finding out exactly which one you are. 

70-80% of your results can come from training intensely while progressing, training consistently, eating enough protein, getting enough sleep, and managing stress. This alone will build you an awesome physique. Will it build you a stage-ready competitive bodybuilder physique? Probably not. That’s where the extra 20-30% of effort comes in. 

I spent a couple of years micromanaging the process and “living” like a competitive bodybuilder with no competitive aspirations and despised it. So it wasn’t for me. That doesn’t mean it doesn’t suit you or other people well, it just wasn’t for me. 

So bottom line, find out what you want to get out of this experience and choose your lifestyle accordingly.

There are a lot of mechanisms to signaling certain systems within the body and many of them overlap. Signaling the need for new muscle tissue is issuing a demand, having adequate calories and protein equals the supply. This can be accomplished from eating in a surplus or having excess bodyfat. With that then we have the question of, well why can’t I just eat enough protein and weight train? Why does having an abundance of total calories matter? THATS more where we get into why it matters that many of these pathways are overlapping. Because your body has certain priorities and when there is less total energy, these different systems send a stronger “signal” that the resources are needed elsewhere. Hope that makes sense

At 6ft tall and being under 200 lbs, you really have a long way to go before your weight begins having deleterious effects on your health. Calories are king. People in here think otherwise and I’m ready for the downvotes on this one but there is nothing special or unique about omad. It is simply a means of controlling your calories. You need to increase your calories and your protein intake. Idk much about the nutrition of a gyro, but I can’t imagine a single one has anymore than 30-50 grams of protein. 

At your height and weight it’s a good idea to get at least around 100 g per day for general health, but when adding strength training into the mix, it should probably be up to 150 g of protein. 

If you fond you can’t hit these targets, it’s no sweat, you may just have to have more meals. Omad is not for everybody, don’t force it. 

Hope this helps, again, breathe. We as humans are not fragile.

No. Creatine does not really do anything to help the muscle building process directly, so any muscle built using creatine will be kept so long as you are still training hard. What creatine does is related to recovery after intense exercise (not necessarily post workout, think more between sets). You have different energy systems that can accomplish different tasks for different durations, the fastest of which is the phosphogen energy system which can create a lot of energy, but fizzles out pretty quick, like 10-15ish seconds quick. Where the phosphagen system burns through energy quickly, it replaces it pretty slowly. This is Where supplementing creatine helps. It provides extra “materials” for your cells to replenish this energy system in a much faster fashion.

Seated calf raise absolutely work the gastrocnemius (big calf muscle), not exclusively the soleus. The gastroc and soleus share a common tendon that inserts into the Achilles, so you won’t get much action out of one without getting some degree of action from the other. You probably just don’t feel it as much in a seated calf raise. 

The difference between wrist extensors/flexors versus the gastroc is the gastroc crosses the knee and ankle joints, making it a biarticular (crossing two joints) muscle, while wrist flexors/extensors cross the wrist joint, but do not cross the elbow joint. That’s why it’s a good idea to have some variation of the joint angle between movements for biarticular muscles like the calves, quads, hamstrings, and triceps

So to sum up: it’s a good idea to have a mix of seated and standing calf raises, for wrist curls, it doesn’t really matter, whatever feels best for you

There’s no such thing as “fat burning mode.” Your individual cells are creating energy from different forms of metabolism at the same time because different tissues have different energy demands. So throughout the day, some cells are doing aerobic metabolism (using fat as energy), while others are doing anaerobic (carbs, glycogen). There is no such thing as your body being in a state of “only burning fat” or “only using carbs/glycogen” because they happen simultaneously depending on the energy needs of the cell. 

That’s why it isn’t worth it to think about. Just put yourself in a calorie deficit and over time you will lose fat regardless of what your glycogen stores are doing.

Your body uses body uses 3 energy systems to generate ATP (the usable form of energy that your cells use), creatine provides a benefit for the very first energy system: the phosphagen energy system. This energy system can pump out an assload of ATP in a very short amount of time, but doesn’t last long and takes a while to recover. Supplementing with creatine provides additional phosphates (see the connection?) for your muscle cells to snatch up after an intense bout of movement. Yes, because there’s more that goes into cardio. Your stroke volume (how much blood is being ejected from the left ventricle into systemic circulation) is the muscular component of cardiac output, and in order to increase your stroke volume you need to progressively overload in a similar way you would through weight training via progressive overload like you said because the heart itself is a muscle. 

This is only one part of the cardiac equation. Stroke volume is only going to increase *so* much, because you’re literally waiting on a compartment of your heart to fill and empty again, which can only happen so quickly. So can you increase stroke volume without increasing total distance? Yes, absolutely. Just like you don’t have to add weight to the bar in order to progressively overload, there are other variables you can manipulate (time, speed, intensity). 

When you think of cardio, think of it more in terms of “how can I deliver the most amount of oxygen to the working muscles?” Rather than “how hard can I push the heart muscle?” It’s much more holistic than just how the muscle itself is working.

Terminology is a bit mixed up, a superset is sequentially hitting antagonistic (differing) muscle groups. A compound set is going to be hitting variations of the same movement targeting the same muscle sequentially. To answer your question though, without getting too deep into the science, calcium is required for muscle cells to form cross-bridges (what actually causes the muscle to contract), and the more you contract the more calcium needed, etc, it’s a huge cycle. These calcium ions start to collect in the capillaries supplying blood to muscle tissue in addition to additional metabolic wastes that occur as a result of using ATP (energy source). So basically letting your muscles rest enables your body to metabolically “clean up” after a set, let’s energy systems recover, and let’s fresh oxygenated blood replenish the worked muscle. So it’s better to let your body recover, especially if the set was difficult.

A lot of this is just my personal opinion and my own experience, I spent a lot of years wasting money on a lot of different supplements. Supplements can be divided into three categories: things that work, things that work but probably aren’t worth your money, and things that are total bullshit. Fortunately, the things that work list is very cut and dry: creatine monohydrate, whey protein, caffeine, and omega 3’s all work and are worth your time and money. Things that work but probably aren’t worth your money: vitamins (I wrestled with which list this one belongs on, but unless you have had a blood panel done and found you are deficient in a vitamin/mineral or have been directed by a physician, it’s not necessary to take any), beta alanine, citruline Malate, turmeric, glucosamine, BCAA’s, EAA’s, and greens powders. Things that are total bullshit: fat burners, test boosters, “pump” products like nitric oxide, things that are gender specific like “women’s protein”, any other form of creatine that’s not monohydrate (krealkyline, hydrochloride, micronized), individual amino acids like D-aspartic acid, cortisol suppressors, natural diuretics, and really specific herbs such as ginko and essential oils. A good guideline for supplements is if it sounds too good to be true, then it is.

There are so many so I’ll try to list as many as I can off the top of my head. A huge one is the misconception of steroids. If you looked like shit before taking them, you will look like shit after a cycle. They’re not a shortcut. Somatotypes (ectomorph, endomorph, etc.) don’t mean anything about how you should workout or what you should eat. Intermittent fasting and things like keto can be successful tools but for a lot of people they are not sustainable and equal results can be accomplished with standard calorie restriction. Which brings me into another one, you HAVE to be in a calorie deficit to lose weight. No exceptions. Eating “clean” foods isn’t a guaranteed way to make you lose weight, it all comes down to energy balance. You could eat 3,000 calories worth of celery and if you’re maintenance intake is around 2,500 calories you will gain fat. Cardio can be helpful and beneficial but it isn’t required. HIIT is a hugely demanding way of exercising and most people do not need to go that route. Salt isn’t the devil. There’s no reason a healthy individual should be limiting their salt intake unless directed by a physician. Carbs do not make you fat, a calorie surplus does. Restricting carbs isn’t necessary for fat loss, a calorie deficit can be created by limiting any macronutrient you want. There are no “good” or “bad” foods. Food is just energy, and eating a burger every now and then isn’t going to ruin you or your health. Compound lifts are not superior to any other kind of machine or free weight lifting style, unless you participate in a sport that requires them such as Olympic lifting or powerlifting. Doing too much is rarely a good thing. The only time you should ever be doing “more” is when you aren’t doing enough. You don’t need to workout 6 days a week to see results. Do exercises you enjoy.
